tip: You ride the subway as a direct object: 지하철을 타요 (jihacheoreul tayo). 타다 (tada = ride) takes 을/를 – no 'on' or 'in'.
몇 (myeot) + a counter asks 'which number': 몇 호선 (myeot hoseon) = 'what number line?'. The same 몇 also asks 'how many'.
Getting off happens AT a place, so it takes 에서: 시청역에서 내려요 (sicheongyeogeseo naeryeoyo). 에서 marks where an action happens – plain 에 won't work here.
Transferring is 'change-riding': 갈아타요 (garatayo) = 갈다 (change) + 타다 (ride). Korean fuses the two verbs into one word.
Korean has no 'have' – things just exist to you: 티머니 카드가 있어요 (timeoni kadeuga isseoyo) is literally 'a T-money card exists'. 있다 covers both 'there is' and 'I have'.
Korean counts big numbers in ten-thousands: 만 원 (man won) = 10,000 won in one syllable. 만 is its own unit – not built as ten × thousand the way English says it.
Korean says 'people are many', not 'there are many people': 사람이 정말 많아요 (sarami jeongmal manayo). The describing verb 많다 (manta) does all the work.
놓치다 (nochida = miss) is for things that get away – 막차를 놓쳤어요 (makchareul nochyeosseoyo). Missing a person uses a completely different verb.
'After' comes after: 10분 후에 (sip-bun hue) is literally '10 minutes after-at'. 후 follows the time span instead of leading it like English 'in ten minutes'.
'There weren't any' is one verb: 자리가 없었어요 (jariga eopseosseoyo) = 'seats not-existed'. 없다 packs 'not' and 'exist' together – no separate negative word.
Korean drops the 'one': 1,500 is 천오백 (cheonobaek), not 일천오백. 천 (cheon = thousand) and 백 (baek = hundred) stand alone when there is just one of them.
도 (do = too) stacks onto other particles: 버스에서도 (beoseueseodo) = 'on the bus too'. 에서 stays put and 도 attaches right after it.
까지 (kkaji) covers both 'to' a place and 'until' a time: 공항까지 (gonghangkkaji = to the airport). One particle does the job of two English words.
There is no word 'traffic' here – the road itself is blocked: 길이 많이 막혀요 (giri mani makyeoyo) = 'the road is really clogged'. That is how Koreans talk about traffic.
Paying is 'calculating': 카드로 계산했어요 (kadeuro gyesanhaesseoyo) = 'I calculated by card'. 계산하다 covers both doing math and settling a bill.
보다 (boda = than) attaches to the thing you compare against: 택시보다 지하철이 싸요 (taeksiboda jihacheori ssayo) runs 'than taxis, the subway is cheap'.
You don't get lost in Korean – you lose the road: 길을 잃어버렸어요 (gireul ireobeoryeosseoyo) = 'I lost the way'. The road is the object, you stay the subject.
저기요 (jeogiyo) is literally 'over there!' – and it is the standard polite way to hail a stranger or a waiter, where English says 'excuse me'.
Position words come after the noun: 은행 앞에서 (eunhaeng apeseo) = 'bank front-at' = in front of the bank. 앞 (ap = front) is a noun that follows what it locates.
한테 (hante = to) marks the person you ask: 직원한테 물어봤어요 (jigwonhante mureobwasseoyo). Questions go 'to' someone – you ask to the staff, not ask the staff.
여행하다 (yeohaenghada = travel) takes a direct object: 한국을 여행했어요 (hangugeul yeohaenghaesseoyo) = 'I traveled Korea' – no 'around' or 'in' needed.
랑 (rang) is the casual spoken 'with': 친구랑 (chingurang = with a friend). In formal writing you would see 와/과 (wa/gwa) instead – same job, different register.
Korean splits 'wear' by body part: 입다 (ipda) for clothes – 한복을 입을 거예요 (hanbogeul ibeul geoyeyo). Shoes take 신다 (sinda), hats 쓰다 (sseuda).
